description.narrative: Lebanon has long been recognized for its rich cultural and religious diversity, as well as its post-war power-sharing arrangements. However, decades of violent and destabilizing events have continuously exposed the fragility and deep-seated fault lines of these arrangements, further straining already complex inter-communal relationships. The Lebanese system has not only weakened the relationship between citizens and the state but has also exacerbated existing inequalities, by the most vulnerable including women, youth, PWDs, and the elderly. In recent years, Lebanon has faced compounded crises, revealing the inadequacies and structural weaknesses of its sectarian power-sharing system. The country has been grappling with the conflict with Israel, the spillover of the Syrian conflict, a severe economic and financial collapse, and a deteriorating socio-political climate. The UNDP Peace Building Project, with a first phase in 2006, has been at the forefront of efforts to tackle the root causes of conflict in Lebanon. The project has consistently worked to create “safe spaces” for local communities to openly discuss their concerns, promote mutual understanding, and strengthen social cohesion. These efforts have targeted various stakeholders, including civil society groups and local public actors. Through participatory and inclusive programs and advocacy initiatives, the project has empowered local stakeholders to play active roles in fostering peace, promoting dialogue, and ensuring a more effective bottom-up approach to peacebuilding. The project shifted its focus in 2013 recognizing the evolving challenges posed by the Syrian refugee crisis and Lebanon’s intensifying socio-political and economic struggles. The project has worked to nurture partnerships between civil society and local government actors, promote collective memory, and integrate peacebuilding concepts into both formal and non-formal educational frameworks.
